Kevin Karplus y Alex Strong publicaron e: Kevin Karplus and Alex Strong published the algorithm in 1983, and had discovered it while looking for something else: a cheap way of making a home computer sound with hardly any memory or multiplications. A buffer of 200 numbers and an average was all they could afford, and out of that came the most convincing string that had been synthesised. Julius Smith and David Jaffe explained that same year why it works: the loop is a simulation of the wave going up and down the string, and the filter, the losses at each bounce. It was the start of physical modelling synthesis, which today simulates whole pianos and clarinets.

The variance of a uniform on $[-1, 1]$ is $\frac{1}{3}$, and its square root, the standard deviation, is the noise's RMS level: 0.577. Compared with a sine of amplitude 1, whose RMS level is $1/\sqrt 2 = 0{.}707$, noise of amplitude 1 sounds somewhat quieter. It is the same old [[pe-descriptiva|variance]] calculation, applied to a list of 44,100 numbers per second.

It reads: “y sub n is noise for the first N samples and, afterwards, g times the average of the outputs from N ago and from N plus one ago”.

The first $N$ samples are the pluck. After that, each sample is the average of the two that sounded one period ago: repeating (the note) and smoothing (the filter) in a single line. The factor $g$, a little less than 1, makes the note die away; with $g = 1$ it would last for ever. The average of two delays by half a sample, and that is why the real period is $N + \frac{1}{2}$: a detail that matters when tuning.

Noise is also used the other way round: to measure. A hi-hat is very high, very short noise. All three are written in two lines each.

Y ahora la sorpresa. Toma un trocito de: And now the surprise. Take a little piece of noise of $N$ samples and repeat it over and over. Since it is periodic, with period $N/f_s$ seconds, it is a note of frequency $f_s/N$, with a rough timbre (all the harmonics at random sizes). Now, on each repetition, replace each sample by the average of two neighbours: the low-pass filter. On each turn a little of the high end is lost, and the note, which started as a crack of noise, keeps smoothing out until it is a pure tone dying away. That is exactly what a plucked string does: the pluck is noise, the high harmonics die first, and the fundamental is left.
